evidence_items.summary: Video saliency prediction is inherently harder to model than static image saliency due to the additional temporal dimension. Video saliency benchmarks rest on the premise that predicting gaze on video requires utilizing temporal activity distributed across frames. Prior work has challenged this, showing that static baselines recover a significant fraction of the explainable gaze information on LEDOV, a popular video saliency dataset, and that video saliency models fail in the same places as this static baseline. We verify that this diagnosis still stands: under a more capable gold standard than the original analysis, and an updated panel of recent architectures, the strongest temporal architecture in the panel still does not substantially improve over a fine-tuned static baseline. However, it remains unclear whether the marginal gain reflects limitations of current temporal architectures or a lack of temporal patterns in the benchmark itself. We introduce SalTempto, a video saliency benchmark with greater dynamism: 224 clips of highly dynamic content, sourced from the HACS-Segments dataset so that each clip contains an event together with its lead-up and aftermath, with gaze recordings from up to 16 subjects and a training split for adapting pretrained models. On SalTempto, the static baseline recovers only about 13\% of the headroom above the centerbias, against more than half on LEDOV. A fine-tuned temporal architecture shows a substantial gain in performance over the static baseline, indicating that it does capture meaningfully more temporal information, which LEDOV fails to measure. Yet, even this SoTA model still leaves nearly half of SalTempto's headroom unexplained, indicating room for improvement in video saliency modelling. Examination of SalTempto also lets us describe human tendencies that models miss. SalTempto link: https://huggingface.co/datasets/bethgelab/video saliency.
evidence_items.title: Moving Forward with Video Saliency: A New Dataset and Benchmark where Motion Matters

evidence_items.summary: Evaluating distributed LLM serving designs on physical clusters is costly. Yet existing simulators provide only subsets of the capabilities needed for realistic design exploration: stateful closed-loop execution, timing prediction without profiling target hardware, and direct execution of unmodified serving benchmarks. We present ServeTwin, a closed-loop simulator that couples specification-driven analytical timing with a stateful serving loop. This coupling captures feedback among request completion, scheduling, queue state, and KV-cache evolution, including prefill-decode disaggregation and multi-turn agent workloads. ServeTwin avoids target-hardware operator profiling through iSTAGE, an analytical trace generator that derives per-iteration traces from model and engine specifications while representing ragged batches and discrete engine mechanisms such as CUDA-graph batch padding. It further decomposes execution time into component-owned throughput, scheduler, and runtime costs. This ownership lets unaffected parameters transfer across platforms and confines recalibration to changed hardware or software components. ServeTwin implements a vLLM-compatible interface and runs unmodified serving benchmarks. Against real deployments, it reproduces InferenceX's steady-state throughput-interactivity frontier with a 3.6% mean error and predicts LMBenchmark's multi-turn performance with a 9.9% error while tracking KV-cache evolution. Pre-silicon sweeps reveal that the preferred HBM bandwidth-capacity tradeoff reverses across workload states and that increasing concurrency shifts the bottleneck from memory bandwidth to scheduler and runtime overheads. Together, these capabilities enable practical exploration of distributed LLM serving systems before target hardware is available.
evidence_items.title: ServeTwin: A Benchmark-Validated Simulator for Distributed LLM Architecture Exploration

organizations: Department of Computer Science and Systems Engineering, Andhra University College of Engineering (A), Visakhapatnam, Andra Pradesh, India.

evidence_items.summary: The 1030-record dataset compiled by Yeh is the de facto benchmark of the concrete strength-prediction literature, and coefficients of determination reported on it routinely exceed 0.90. This study shows that part of that reported accuracy reflects the internal structure of the dataset rather than predictive capability. The 1030 records describe only 427 distinct mix proportions: one batch is cast and then tested at several curing ages, so that 76.1 per cent of records share their composition with at least one other record that differs only in age. Under the random partitioning used almost universally in this literature, models are therefore evaluated on mixes already seen during training. Five estimators spanning a range of flexibility are re-evaluated under random and mix-grouped five-fold cross-validation, each repeated ten times. The mix-grouped protocol lowers R² for every estimator, but unevenly: the reduction is negligible for ordinary least squares (0.002) and k-nearest neighbours (0.004) and material for support-vector regression (0.029), random forest (0.043) and gradient boosting (0.054). The apparent advantage of gradient boosting over least squares is consequently overstated by about 19 per cent. The penalty is concentrated in the sparsely sampled high-strength region (60 MPa and above), whose records are also the most heavily replicated; there, the root-mean-square error of the two tree ensembles rises by 42 and 44 per cent. A controlled experiment on synthetic data with a known generative law and a tunable per-mix batch effect confirms the mechanism: the gap is zero without a batch effect and grows monotonically with it. The study concludes that leakage-aware evaluation, rather than synthetic augmentation, is the appropriate corrective, and provides a single executable notebook that reproduces every result.
evidence_items.title: Quantifying Evaluation Bias in Machine Learning Models for Concrete Compressive Strength: Mix-Level Replication in the Yeh Benchmark and Its Differential Effect on Model Comparison

evidence_items.summary: Data accompanying N. Vauquier, B. M. L. Srivastava, S. A. Hosseini and E. Vincent, "Legally validated evaluation framework for voice anonymization", Interspeech 2025, pages 3229 to 3233, doi:10.21437/Interspeech.2025-1699. The paper introduces two metrics, Singling Out and Linkability, that translate the singling out and linkability criteria of the Article 29 Working Party's Opinion 05/2014 on Anonymization Techniques into quantities that can be measured on speech. The framework was formally validated by the French Data Protection Authority (CNIL). This record holds the data needed to reproduce the paper's results. The reference implementation is at https://github.com/brijmohan/voice-anonymization-legal-eval CONTENTS Dataset definitions, unchanged from version 1.0.0: cv11-A-filelist (19.5 MB): the Mozilla Common Voice 11.0 clips forming subset A, 22,024 speakers with at least 2 minutes of speech each. cv11-B-filelist (83.3 MB): the clips forming subset B, 4,949 speakers with at least 3 minutes each. Subset B's speakers are a subset of A's, with disjoint utterances. Cosine score matrices, new in version 2.0.0, 12 files totalling 5.2 GB: scores L .npy: a 22,024 x 4,949 float32 array per attacker model and conversation length. Entry [i, j] is the cosine similarity between enrollment speaker i of subset A and test speaker j of subset B. scores L .npy.json: a sidecar per matrix giving the row and column speaker order, so each matrix is self describing. MANIFEST.json: SHA-256 checksums and shapes for every file. The four attacker models differ in what their speaker embedding extractor was trained on: original: original speech, evaluated on original speech. ignorant: original speech. semi informed: speech anonymized with VoicePrivacy 2022 baseline B1.a. informed: speech anonymized with VoicePrivacy 2024 baseline B1. Conversation length L is the number of utterances averaged per speaker, and takes the values 1, 3 and 30.
evidence_items.title: Score matrices and dataset definitions for "Legally validated evaluation framework for voice anonymization" (Interspeech 2025)

evidence_items.summary: Curated, high-confidence structural and functional gene annotation of Phytophthora plurivora strain TJ71 (release 2), provided in GFF3 and GTF formats (15,363 gene models; gene, mRNA, exon and CDS features), together with the encoded proteins and coding sequences. The annotation was generated with a BRAKER3-based structural prediction pipeline, followed by a custom curation workflow combining transcript deduplication, repeat- and expression-aware filtering, a heuristic homology-and-topology scoring scheme, directed manual curation and an audit of overlapping gene models supported by RNA-seq evidence. This dataset was produced as part of the associated manuscript describing the curated gene catalogue of P. plurivora and its expression during host infection. Release 2 supersedes release 1 (15,415 gene models): 84 redundant, chimeric or read-through models were removed, and 31 loci were reinstated. Identifiers of release 1 are preserved; the reinstated loci carry new identifiers (PPLU 15416 to PPLU 15446), and the identifiers of removed models are retired and not re-used. This annotation is built on the previously published genome assembly available at NCBI GenBank under accession GCA 030027945.1 (ASM3002794v1). The genome FASTA itself is not included in this deposit. See the accompanying README release2.md for a full description of the files, the changes from release 1 and the identifier conventions.
evidence_items.title: Curated gene annotation of Phytophthora plurivora TJ71 (release 2): GFF3, GTF, proteins and coding sequences

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Objectives The primary objective was to evaluate the predictive performance of artificial intelligence (AI) models for craniofacial and mandibular growth prediction. Secondary objectives were to assess methodological quality and identify research gaps. Materials and methods Nine databases were searched through August 12, 2026, supplemented by manual searches. Human studies assessing AI-based models for craniofacial or mandibular growth prediction were included. Study characteristics, prediction intervals, AI approaches, performance metrics, and validation strategies were extracted. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed using PROBAST. Results Twelve studies were included. Six assessed overall craniofacial growth, whereas six mandibular development. Prediction horizons ranged from ≤ 1.5 to approximately 10 years, with sample sizes of 33–639 participants. Predictive accuracy varied by anatomical region and methodological approach. Sex and malocclusion type were frequently used to define study populations but were not consistently incorporated as predictors, whereas ethnicity and skeletal maturation were rarely considered. Seven studies had overall high risk of bias and five unclear risk, mainly due to analytical limitations and inadequate validation. Conclusion AI-based models show promising predictive performance; however, current evidence is insufficient to establish superiority over traditional statistical methods. Overall high or unclear risk of bias and substantial heterogeneity in study populations and datasets, prediction horizons, outcome definitions, and AI modelling approaches limit confidence in the findings. Standardized multicenter datasets and independent external validation are required before clinical implementation. Clinical relevance AI-based growth prediction may support individualized orthodontic diagnosis and treatment timing, but current evidence does not support routine clinical use.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence for craniofacial and mandibular growth prediction: A systematic review

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Acute ischemic stroke is a major cause of disability and death worldwide, and the key to its treatment lies in seizing every minute. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) technologies represented by deep learning and machine learning have shown potential in improving the efficiency and accuracy of diagnosing and treating this disease. This paper aims to systematically review the application progress of AI throughout the whole chain of diagnosing and treating acute ischemic stroke, including early identification and early—warning, precise imaging evaluation (such as distinguishing the infarct core from the ischemic penumbra), optimization of treatment decisions, as well as prognosis and rehabilitation management. This paper analyzes the applications and clinical values of current AI models, and deeply explores the problems it faces in terms of data quality, model generalization, clinical interpretability, and ethics and regulations, providing a theoretical basis and guiding direction for promoting acute ischemic stroke into an era of intelligent and personalized diagnosis and treatment.
evidence_items.title: Research progress of artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and treatment of acute ischemic stroke

organizations: advanced institute of industrial technology, Tokyo, Japan
evidence_items.summary: Natural material touch combines kinesthetic motion, contact resistance, vibration, visible deformation, and sound. Dry sand is a difficult case for smartphone-mediated touch because granular contact produces broadband friction-induced vibration and material displacement, whereas a phone provides a rigid glass surface and a constrained vibration pathway. We present a preliminary signal-level benchmark for dry-sand material interaction across phone-surface output routes. Using a gravity-loaded contact-shoe rig with a load cell and an ADXL1002 analog MEMS accelerometer, we measure dry silica sand No. 5 under two nominal total contact-load conditions and compare it with an empty-container control. We then evaluate two output routes on the same phone surface: an auxiliary surface exciter attached to the phone body, treated as a reproduction-oriented route, and the built-in linear resonant actuator driven by envelope-based Android vibration commands, treated as an approximation route. Real dry-sand traces concentrate most energy above 1 kHz, with a stable median frequency near 2.2 kHz. The auxiliary exciter partially preserves the kHz-range frequency location but reshapes the spectral distribution, whereas the built-in actuator collapses output around 164 Hz and leaves little supra-kHz energy. The contribution is not a perceptual-equivalence claim. Instead, the benchmark identifies which vibrotactile evidence is preserved, reshaped, or lost, and uses that receiver-aware loss profile to formulate future multimodal compensation hypotheses.
evidence_items.title: Beyond the Vibration Channel: A Signal-Level Benchmark for Dry-Sand Touch on Phones

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in document key–value pair(KVP) extraction, yet controlled evaluations of their robustness to optical character recognition (OCR)output remain limited. This leaves an important gap in understanding their reliability within real-world OCR-to-LLM pipelines. Unlike end-to-end Vision-Language Models (VLMs) that conflate visualperception with semantic extraction, modular pipelines allow errors to be explicitly isolated andaudited. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce a controlled, large-scale benchmarking frameworkdesigned to distinguish downstream LLM extraction behavior from upstream OCR degradation. Thisbenchmark evaluates 136 experimental configurations and 17,688 deterministic document-level inferenceinstances across five instruction-tuned open-weight LLMs (2B–8B parameters), three complementarydatasets, and four text-quality conditions. This extensive matrix pairs a full zero-shot comparisonand targeted one- to three-shot experiments with a confirmatory sensitivity analysis comprising 40configurations across 20 frozen demonstration sets. By separating Key Recall (annotated-field recovery)from Exact Match and Value F1 (exact and partial value recovery, respectively), we reveal whetherOCR degradation affects field identification and value reproduction differently across models. Crucially,our findings challenge three practical evaluation assumptions: (1) that clean-text performance is areliable proxy for real-world robustness, (2) that model rankings remain consistent across annotation-derived Gold and OCR-derived text conditions, and (3) that providing few-shot demonstrationsmonotonically improves extraction accuracy. By exposing vulnerabilities such as model-rankingreversals and unstable few-shot gains, this benchmark provides a rigorous and reproducible frameworkfor evaluating LLM reliability under noisy document conditions.
evidence_items.title: From Pixels to Pairs: A Comprehensive Benchmark of LLM-Driven Key–Value Extraction in Noisy Document Settings
Quality, safety, and readability of consumer-facing generative AI responses to end-of-life questions relevant to surrogate decision-makers for older adults: a benchmark evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Big Data is becoming an important component of modern agronomy by enabling the integration, processing and analysis of large, diverse and continuously generated datasets for improved agricultural decision-making. Agricultural Big Data is generated from multiple sources, including remote sensing satellites, Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs), Internet of Things (IoT) sensors, weather stations, farm machinery, field observations and historical databases. The integration of these data sources with Geographic Information Systems (GIS), cloud computing, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) enables the identification of spatial and temporal patterns that are difficult to detect using conventional approaches. Big Data applications in agronomy include climate and weather prediction, pest and disease management, soil health and nutrient management, irrigation scheduling, crop yield prediction, precision agriculture, crop insurance and weed management. Examples from India and other regions demonstrate the application of satellite imagery, UAV-based sensing, IoT systems, crop-growth models and machine-learning algorithms for field-scale and regional agricultural decision making. Big Data analytics can improve resource-use efficiency, support predictive and real-time monitoring, strengthen agricultural risk assessment and facilitate site-specific management. However, effective implementation is constrained by challenges such as high infrastructure and operational costs, data quality and interoperability issues, data privacy and ownership concerns, limited rural digital infrastructure, inadequate technical skills and increasing requirements for data storage and computing. Therefore, the effective integration of Big Data with agronomic knowledge and decision-support systems can contribute to more precise, efficient and sustainable agricultural production while addressing emerging challenges related to climate variability, resource scarcity and food security.
evidence_items.title: BIG DATA IN AGRONOMY: TECHNOLOGIES,  APPLICATIONS, BENEFITS AND CHALLENGES

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence agents now search, evaluate, negotiate, and pay on behalf of consumers, while firms deploy agents that create content, personalize offers, and complete transactions. Agentic commerce therefore weakens a foundational assumption of marketing thought and marketing measurement: that the recipient of marketing activity is a human being. The evidence is scattered across marketing, information systems, computer science, economics, and law, and it has a largely forgotten first act in the shopbot research of the late 1990s. Following the SPAR-4-SLR protocol with PRISMA 2020 reporting, we screen 5,157 records from Scopus, Web of Science, and EBSCO Business Source and add verified snowballing to assemble 140 primary studies spanning 1994 to 2026. Each study is coded on influence direction, customer journey stage, delegation depth, method, and research wave. The synthesis yields an actor taxonomy with a five-level delegation ladder, an influence triad that separates marketing to, through, and by agents, an integrated account of trust and governance infrastructure, and a market-level analysis connecting both research waves. The Agentic Commerce Reference Framework consolidates this evidence into four auditable layers with explicit cross-layer dynamics, a ten-proposition research agenda, and five measurement instruments for analytics practice. A complete replication package accompanies the article.
evidence_items.title: When the customer is a machine: a systematic literature review and integrative framework of agentic commerce

organizations: School of Computer Science and Engineering, Vellore Institute of Technology
Department of Electrical and Electronic Engineering, UCSI University
evidence_items.summary: Conventional maternal remote patient monitoring has relied upon using immutable ranges for detection of conditions on maternal telemetry. However, this has created extreme alert fatigue in clinicians. The newly proposed Agentic AI Maternal Triage Framework combines patient-reported outcome data with quantitative telemetry values to deliver real-time, context-aware decisions regarding risk stratification to both the clinician and patient. The triage workloads are processed in an orchestrated manner via n8n, utilizing light gradient boosting machine models to determine the likelihood that the maternal telemetry is showing that the patient is developing cardiovascular or metabolic risks. The models produce continuous risk scores that are consumed by a retrieval-augmented generation-powered Google Gemini large language model to yield structured triaged outputs. The triage outputs are delivered to a conversational agent for low-risk patients and a physician for high-risk patients using a triage model of escalation. To allow for continued learning, expert validation is captured via stateless webhooks. In the simulation-based evaluation, the predictive models achieved classification metrics above 99.8%; however, these results reflect the controlled synthetic data-generating environment and do not establish clinical validity. The framework therefore represents a technical proof of concept for integrating predictive modeling, retrieval-grounded generative reasoning, context-aware routing, and human-in-the-loop feedback, with external clinical validation required before real-world deployment.
evidence_items.title: An agentic AI- and n8n automation-powered maternal care framework with predictive pregnancy monitoring and continuous learning

organizations: CSAIL, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, Massachusetts, USA
MIT Lincoln Laboratory, Lexington, Massachusetts, USA
evidence_items.summary: Maps are central to how humans make sense of the world, from navigation and environmental monitoring to military planning and historical interpretation. Yet despite rapid progress in large multimodal models (LMMs), these systems continue to struggle with interpreting maps – an essential skill for visual reasoning that goes beyond pattern recognition and text extraction. To further progress toward this capability, we introduce MapQA, the first large-scale benchmark specifically designed to evaluate LMMs on map understanding. MapQA contains over 9,700 carefully curated, open-ended question–answer pairs spanning diverse map types, each constructed to require reasoning directly from the map rather than relying on memorized world knowledge. Benchmark questions were generated through a scalable human-in-the-loop process to ensure quality, and evaluated using an LLM-as-a-judge protocol aligned with human judgments. Our experiments show that while humans answer over 91% of questions correctly, state-of-the-art proprietary models achieve barely a third of that performance, with open-source models below 30%. These findings highlight a substantial gap between human and machine map understanding, underscoring the need for benchmarks like MapQA to guide future progress in multimodal reasoning.
evidence_items.title: MapQA: A Map-Question-Answering Benchmark for Visual Language Model Reasoning

organizations: School of Science and Technology, Hong Kong Metropolitan University, Hong Kong, China
School of Data Science, Lingnan University, Hong Kong, China
evidence_items.summary: Personality-aware Human-Computer Dialogue (HCD) systems are critical for enabling personalized interactions. However, to the best of our knowledge, existing HCD benchmarks lack explicit personality trait annotations, creating a fundamental barrier to developing robust personality-aware HCD systems. To address this, we introduce Big5-HCD, the first HCD benchmark with fine-grained Big Five personality annotations. This benchmark was derived from RealPersonaChat—a Human-Human Dialogue (HHD) benchmark—through a four-stage semi-supervised pipeline: (1) Construction of a subset based on sampling of HHDs from RealPersonaChat; (2) Construction of role-model HCDs with validation by human evaluators; (3) Construction of a human-calibrated Large Language Model (LLM) evaluation benchmark for automatic adaptation; and (4) Adapation based on LLM evaluators’ consensus for HCD scaling. Experimental evaluations of adaptation effectiveness on Big5-HCD showed high approval rates and tolerance scores from human evaluators, confirming its reliability as a personality-annotated HCD benchmark for developing personality-aware HCD systems. The source code and data are available in: https://github.com/Drew19980118/Big5-HCD.git.
evidence_items.title: Big5-HCD: A Human-Computer Dialogue Benchmark with Personality Annotations via Semi-Supervised Adaptation

evidence_items.summary: Medical diagnosis often benefits from the side-by-side analysis of different sources of information, motivating also the development of multimodal approaches in AI-based applications for healthcare. A current technique for vision-language multimodality is a two-step process of (1) image tokenization through vector quantization followed by (2) auto-regressive modeling. In this work, we explore the image tokenization process for datasets in the medical domain, which are characterized by smaller scale and narrower semantic coverage than natural image datasets. We benchmark both reconstruction quality, codebook collapse and representational capacity of VQ-VAEs across a variety of settings, surpassing state of the art in the reconstruction task and providing a stepping stone for further development of medical multimodal auto-regressive techniques.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Vector Quantized Auto-Encoders for Multimodal Vision-Language Tokenization of Medical Images

evidence_items.summary: Climate misinformation on social media often combines misleading headlines with professional-looking maps, increasing the perceived credibility of false or decontextualized claims. As users increasingly rely on multimodal large language models (MLLMs) for credibility support, they may encounter either consistent or conflicting recommendations from multiple AI assistants. This ongoing study examines how people evaluate headline-map climate change misinformation under parallel and independent guidance from multiple MLLMs. Using eight real climate-related social media posts, we designed an interactive interface in which 26 participants rated the credibility of headlines and maps while receiving parallel assessments from ChatGPT 5 and Gemini 2.5 Pro, with options to inspect model reasoning and engage in follow-up dialogue. Preliminary findings show that consistent MLLMs guidance reduced variation in human credibility assessments, especially for misinformation headlines: when both models agreed that a headline was unreliable, participants tended to align with the consensus and provide strongly negative ratings. In contrast, inconsistent MLLMs guidance generated greater uncertainty and variation in human credibility assessments. Under conflicting MLLMs guidance, participants did not simply average model scores; instead, their judgments shifted toward neutrality and avoided extreme ratings. Analysis of user–MLLMs dialogue further shows that participants used the models to clarify scientific concepts, trace sources, and interpret map-based evidence.
evidence_items.title: How Humans Evaluate Headline-Map Climate Change Misinformation with Multi-Agent (In)consistent Guidance?

evidence_items.summary: Misogyny in multimodal memes is difficult to identify because the insult often lives in culturally specific implication rather than in the image or text alone. The same visual-textual pairing may read as hostile in one community and harmless in another. Standard multimodal classifiers, which tend to compress pixels and tokens into a single latent space, have limited means to represent these regional disagreements. We address the Cross-Cultural Misogynistic Meme Detection (CC-MMD) challenge with the Structured Cross-Cultural Multi-Agent Cognitive Architecture (SC-MACA). The system first uses a Large Vision-Language Model to run an Objective-Cultural-Judge (O-C-J) pipeline, turning ambiguous meme cues into structured cultural interpretations. These interpretations are then fused by a Consensus-Deviation Decomposition Architecture (CDDA), which separates shared cross-cultural evidence from culture-specific departures before classification. A masked training objective handles missing native labels, while an auxiliary severity head preserves the four misogyny dimensions used by the judge agent. On the official Task B leaderboard, SC-MACA obtains an overall Macro-F1 of 0.8155, with especially strong results on the low-resource Malayalam partition (F1 = 0.9117).
evidence_items.title: neucsestu@CC-MMD 2026: SC-MACA via Multi-Agent Cultural Reasoning for Misogyny Detection

evidence_items.summary: Turn-taking and backchanneling are governed by culture-specific display rules: the same listener behavior that signals attentive engagement in one language community can read as interruption or disengagement in another. As large language models (LLMs), often accessed as multimodal systems, are increasingly deployed as evaluators of conversational behavior, it is unclear whether their judgments encode such culture-specific norms or default to a single, implicitly English-language, interactional standard. We introduce a lightweight probing protocol that isolates cultural bias using parallel dialogue: identical conversational content aligned across four languages (English, German, Italian, Chinese) from the XDailyDialog corpus. Holding content fixed, we elicit LLM judgments of turn-appropriateness, response naturalness, and speaker engagement, and measure how these judgments shift with the language and stated cultural framing of the interlocutors. On a text-only open-weight model, we find that identical dialogues are rated significantly more appropriate and more engaged in German and Italian than in English (drifts up to + 0.49 on a 5-point scale), and that merely relabeling a dialogue’s culture, without changing its words, can lower its rating by more than a point, isolating the effect of the cultural label from that of the content. The drift is stable across repeated sampling but differs in direction across models, indicating that current LLMs assess turn-taking through a monocultural, model-specific lens.
evidence_items.title: Judging Turn-Taking Through a Monocultural Lens: A Parallel-Corpus Probe of Cultural Bias in LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as primary information sources, raising critical concerns about their safety and reliability across languages. While prior work has established the importance of harmless yet non-evasive responses, these guarantees are largely evaluated in high-resource languages. In this paper, we investigate the safety of responses in LLMs in Sinhala, a low-resource language with strong cultural grounding. We introduce a framework that extends existing definitions of harmlessness by incorporating responsible behaviour, requiring models to actively discourage harmful actions and provide safety-oriented guidance for culturally grounded question prompts. Using a curated set of culturally grounded and safety-critical queries, we evaluate multiple publicly available LLMs across categories, including self-harm, medical advice, culturally sensitive topics, and illegal activities. Our findings reveal significant safety gaps, including the generation of dangerous misinformation and the absence of appropriate intervention in high-risk scenarios. We further propose a Sinhala-specific diagnostic dataset to evaluate the safety of responses generated by LLMs in the Sinhala language.
evidence_items.title: Towards Responsible AI in Low-Resource Languages: Evaluating LLM Responses with a Culturally Aware Sinhala Dataset

evidence_items.summary: Generative image models can support instructional visual content, but safety-relevant automotive imagery requires more than photorealism: generated scenes must preserve cockpit geometry, human-machine-interface (HMI) iconography, and physically plausible vehicle behavior. We evaluate a two-stage pipeline in which large language models (LLMs) extend technical owner-manual descriptions and reference-image constraints into downstream image-generation prompts, across four Cadillac LYRIQ advanced driver assistance system (ADAS) scenarios. Using a factorial design over prompt-extension LLM, thinking mode, injected Chain-of-Thought (CoT) source, prompt style, scenario, and image generator, we collect N = 18, 551 manually rated images (Excellent/Good/Fair/Poor). The downstream generator was the dominant quality determinant: Nano Banana Pro and Nano Banana 2 produced 16.9% and 14.3% usable images, whereas GPT-Image-1.5 produced 0.5% and collapsed to near-uniform failure. Within the viable Google generators, LLM and CoT effects were generator- and scenario-dependent; because both viable generators are Google, the CoT-source effect reflects trace–generator alignment (Google-aligned CoT helped, OpenAI-sourced CoT hurt) rather than a general CoT benefit. A robustness analysis further reveals a trade-off between high-performing specialist and lower-variance generalist configurations. Domain-constrained instructional image generation should therefore be evaluated as a coupled system spanning generator, prompt-extension model, reasoning trace, prompt template, and scenario.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking Prompt Extension and Image Generation Models for Automotive Instructional Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Analyzing multi-party physical collaboration means tracking what a group builds and whether their actions move the shared structure toward a goal. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) could automate this analysis from session recordings, but existing spatial-reasoning benchmarks use rendered scenes or curated snapshots, not real collaborative video. We present STACK, to our knowledge the first benchmark pairing real multi-party construction video with dense 3D annotations and goal-paired judgment. Using 237 keyframes from 19 LEGO sessions, we evaluate seven VLMs across input modality, structural complexity, and manipulation judgment. A structured JSON state drives reconstruction accuracy to near-perfect across all models. Rendered views outperform real video frames, while additional viewpoints give only marginal gains. For manipulation judgment, frontier models reach 80–92% accuracy while open 7–8B models stay at chance. A key dissociation emerges. Small open models identify what manipulation happened with structured context but cannot judge whether the result is spatially correct. These findings expose a gap between perception and judgment in current VLMs and inform their use as analyzers of collaborative group dynamics.
evidence_items.title: STACK: 3D Spatial Task Analysis in Collaborative Construction Keyframes

evidence_items.summary: The Context-Aware Student Engagement Detection (CASED) Challenge introduces a benchmark for estimating student engagement from short online lecture clips by integrating behavioral cues with instructor activity and lecture context. CASED contains 8,472 ten-second clips from 72 students, with a participant-independent split of 4,978 training clips from 43 students and 3,494 test clips from 29 unseen students. The challenge defines two tracks: continuous engagement estimation and binary engaged/disengaged classification. This paper presents the benchmark construction, released modalities and metadata, label-generation process, evaluation protocol, and six accepted submissions. The submitted approaches explored uncertainty-aware multimodal fusion, transformer-based models, multimodal language models, gradient boosting, multi-task learning, and zero-shot prompting. Despite their diverse designs, the systems achieved comparable performance, with limited generalization to unseen students. The results suggest that scaling models and incorporating additional modalities alone are insufficient, highlighting the importance of identity robustness, uncertainty modeling, and reliable validation for engagement estimation.
evidence_items.title: SMART Challenge Series: Context-Aware Student Engagement Detection Challenge

evidence_items.summary: Dynamic power cables (DPC) are a common, yet complex component used in offshore renewable energy systems such as floating offshore wind farms/turbines. However, their dynamic torsional behavior has not yet been contemplated. Hence, this paper develops an effective numerical approach using a simplified, scaled-down finite element (FE) model to predict the dynamic torsional behavior of a 24 kV dynamic power cable, thus addressing the scarcity of torsion-focused FE studies. This work is the first study to develop a FE model for this specific type of innovative cable design introduced by Nordiske Kabel og Traadfabriker (NKT). Exclusive torsion and traction data are acquired in this work to validate and calibrate the numerical model. These datasets can also serve as references for cable designers and engineers to validate, benchmark, or develop their own FE models. The objective of the study is determine the torsional stiffness of the cable, a critical mechanical property required during the early design stage. The FE model was developed in ABAQUS software and calibrated through experimental traction and torsion testing performed at Université Gustave Eiffel in France. The numerical domain was reduced to a representative section of the cable, enabling efficient modelling while preserving the dominant mechanical interactions and physics. To ensure validity of the developed model, its results were compared with both experimental data and analytical stress calculations which revealed good agreement across all approaches. The study demonstrates that accurate contact modelling is crucial and that a simplified FE approach can be employed in the initial stages as a cost and time-efficient alternative to experimental testing for prediction of torsional characteristics of DPCs. Methodologies for further reduction of the computational domain is currently under investigation.
evidence_items.title: An Efficient Approach for Modelling Dynamic Torsional Behavior of a Complex Marine Power Cable

evidence_items.summary: Hand gestures are a natural and expressive modality for human communication and are increasingly used in multimodal interaction, including human-computer interaction, extended reality, robotics, assistive technologies, and embodied AI. However, designing robust gesture-based interfaces remains challenging due to issues related to gesture acquisition, tracking quality, continuous recognition, semantic interpretation, ergonomics, and real-time deployment. In this tutorial, we will present methods and challenges involved in developing effective gestural interaction systems. We will first introduce the role of hand gestures in multimodal interaction and discuss how gestures can complement other modalities such as speech, gaze, body motion, and object interaction. We will then present current technologies for hand and finger tracking, including vision-based, sensor-based, and wearable approaches, with a focus on their limitations in terms of accuracy, robustness, latency, and data quality. A central part of the tutorial will focus on hand gesture recognition, covering segmented and continuous recognition, gesture representations, learning-based methods, benchmarks, and tools for real-time recognition. We will also introduce recent advances in hand motion generation, with emphasis on multimodal conditioning from text, audio, body motion, and objects, as well as key challenges related to realism, physical plausibility, and real-time performance. Overall, the tutorial will provide participants with a concise but comprehensive view of how hand gestures can be captured, recognized, interpreted, and generated in multimodal interactive systems.
evidence_items.title: Using Hand Gestures for Multimodal Interactions: Foundations, Methods, and Emerging Challenges
GENEA Workshop 2026: The 7th Workshop on Generation and Evaluation of Non-verbal Behaviour for Embodied Agents

evidence_items.summary: Ordinary digital games are typically controlled through low-movement inputs such as touch, keyboards, or gamepads, limiting embodied and adaptive interaction. We present a personalized embodied control layer that allows users to remap ordinary games through self-defined body poses and short motions captured with commodity mobile devices. The system supports user-specific pose recording, lightweight temporal modeling, partial landmark tolerance, and cross-platform command realization for Android touch gestures and desktop keyboard input. We evaluate the approach through a technical benchmark and a within-subject user study. The benchmark shows that the pipeline is feasible for interactive use on commodity hardware, achieving strong recognition performance and low end-to-end latency. In the user study, we did not detect significant differences between self-defined and imposed mappings on the primary objective or subjective measures. In contrast, performance and ratings improved consistently across rounds, indicating that early use was shaped strongly by familiarization. Interviews nevertheless suggested that many participants experienced self-defined mappings as more natural and intuitive. Together, these findings position personalized embodied control as a practical cross-platform interaction layer for ordinary games, identify familiarization as the clearest empirical factor shaping first-session use, and generate the hypothesis that the benefits of personalization may emerge after users move beyond the earliest familiarization phase.
evidence_items.title: Pose-to-Command: A Personalized Embodied Control Layer for Ordinary Games

evidence_items.summary: Situated LLM assistants increasingly receive mobile and smart-environment signals, yet many expose the same tools and memory sources across physical scenes. We present scene-conditioned capability mounting, in which a resolved scene determines the resources shown to the planner. Stale resources are removed before planning, while independent runtime gates check proposed tool calls and memory reads. In a controlled two-scene benchmark, dynamic mounting reduced a character-based estimate of tool-schema prompt size from 676 to 288–289 estimated token equivalents (about 57%). Runtime gates yielded no completed cross-scene action in 520 contaminated runs and no cross-scene memory return in 1,200 read-side runs within the evaluated threat model. We also conducted a 24-participant fixed-task prototype study in which scripted scene states controlled authorization while BLE signals were logged as telemetry. Every cross-scene trial displayed a blocked cue and produced no cross-scene action or memory content; interview coding showed that the appropriate repair remained unclear after some boundary events. Together, the studies connect planner exposure and runtime authorization to the boundary cues shown in the interface. The benchmark provides mechanism-level evidence, while the prototype identifies interaction requirements for presenting scripted boundary transitions.
evidence_items.title: Scene-Conditioned Capability Mounting as a Visible and Executable Boundary for Situated LLM Agents

evidence_items.summary: As multimodal interaction becomes central to digital learning, technical interfaces, such as eBooks and conversational agents, present unique accessibility challenges for users relying on the auditory modality. While modern Text-to-Speech (TTS) systems excel at rendering natural language, they often fail to convey the complex, structural syntax of source code, creating a significant barrier for blind and low-vision programmers. We frame the vocal rendering of source code as a cross-modal translation task, in which spatial and symbolic information visually encoded in code must be mapped into a linear auditory signal. This study explores "Code-to-Speech" (CTS) as a critical component of multimodal technical communication. We present a comparative evaluation of five leading AI-driven TTS engines (including ChatGPT, Gemini, and ElevenLabs) to determine their efficacy in rendering mixed-content (text and code) materials. Adopting a mixed-methods approach, we combine automated linguistic metrics (WER, BLEU, METEOR) with a human-centered qualitative assessment. Our findings reveal significant differences: ChatGPT and Gemini consistently achieved lower error rates, while Copilot omitted critical tokens. However, all systems struggle with essential structural cues such as indentation, pauses, and code comments. We also show that designed prompts improve intelligibility, particularly for novices. Our work establishes a benchmark for CTS and underscores the need for multimodal AI architectures that support inclusive technical interaction.
evidence_items.title: Code-to-Speech: An Exploratory Study of AI Text-to-Speech for Source Code Readability

evidence_items.summary: Humor is a fundamental component of human interaction, and integrating it into multimodal systems is crucial for developing more natural and socio-affective conversational agents. However, humor detection remains challenging due to the subjective, multimodal, and temporally fluid nature of comedic events. In this work, we present a comprehensive framework for humor detection, utilizing a highly curated multilingual stand-up comedy dataset. We first propose a robust, unsupervised acoustic laughter segmentation model to generate precise labels, overcoming the acoustic limitations of idealized datasets. Using laughter as a proxy, we reframe humor detection as a causal, word-level sequence labeling task. We introduce a multimodal architecture that fuses textual, acoustic, and visual skeletal features, demonstrating that this integration outperforms unimodal baselines. Furthermore, to address the shortcomings of traditional sequence metrics that penalize minor temporal offsets, we establish specialized evaluation metrics derived from a systematic PRISMA literature review. Our findings underscore the necessity of multimodal integration and provide a standardized evaluation setup for future humor research.
evidence_items.title: Decoding Humor in Stand-up Comedy: A Multilingual and Multimodal Sequence Labeling Approach

evidence_items.summary: While research on generative multimodal social agents has recently gained interest, cultural aspects of non-verbal behaviour and gesture generation remain relatively unexplored. Research has especially neglected the evaluation of these culture-specific aspects, focusing instead on general measures of behavioural appropriateness, naturalness and speech alignment. Based on the literature and our own experience, we discuss several important aspects that future evaluations should consider. We examine evaluation processes that can be replicated to analyse generative performance in a culture-sensitive manner. The paper focuses on evaluation constructs such as cultural recognizability, social acceptance, behavioural fidelity, human behavioural response, and cultural understanding, and considers what measurements could assess these constructs, such as standardized questionnaires and uniform computed metrics.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Cross-Cultural Generative Embodied Social Agents

evidence_items.summary: Creating expressive, human-like virtual agents requires the synthesis of meaningful co-speech gestures. However, automatically generating semantically appropriate gestures remains challenging, in part because the role and meaning of various gesture forms is not well understood. Clustering gesture forms offers a promising way to structure the gesture space, but remains underexplored. In this work, we investigate semantic clustering of co-speech gestures using both classical and deep learning-based approaches, applied to a newly labeled dataset and evaluated under external validation. Since the usage of gesture forms varies considerably in spontaneous speech, any dataset is inherently imbalanced. To address this, we propose a hybrid deep embedded clustering approach with a nearest-neighbor-graph-based initialization strategy to discover clusters that are consistent with the imbalanced distribution of gesture categories. We compare a range of feature representations—including wrist-path dynamics, palm orientation, and hand shape—combined with multiple embedding strategies that include Raw features, UMAP, a Transformer autoencoder, a Vector Quantized VAE (VQVAE), and our hybrid deep clustering approach. Our results show that feature choice is the dominant factor in clustering performance, consistently outweighing the impact of the dimensionality-reduction method. In particular, compact morphological features capturing wrist-path dynamics and palm orientation produce the most robust and transferable cluster structure across datasets. In contrast, higher-dimensional representations based on full joint configurations are less effective for unsupervised semantic clustering.
evidence_items.title: Clustering Co-Speech Gestures Using Morphological Representations

evidence_items.summary: Breathing plays a fundamental role in speech production and perception, providing important cues about the speaker’s physical and psychological state. Recently, the use of breathing as a cognitive, affective, and physical marker has gained momentum, especially in the fields of speech synthesis, conversational robots and agents. However, the challenges associated with breathing annotation and the lack of annotated datasets for these purposes hinders further progress. Automatic breathing signal prediction could bridge this gap. Unfortunately, state-of-the-art (SOTA) research in this area remains difficult to replicate due to the lack of openly available code or datasets. This work makes four key contributions: (1) we implement previously proposed SOTA methods for speech-based breathing prediction, explicitly stating any assumptions made; (2) we introduce extensions to improve their performance; (3) we propose two novel WavLM-based models; and (4) we evaluate the impact of speaker-specific conditioning via feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), using speaker embeddings (eGeMAPS and WeSpeaker) to modulate intermediate representations. To ensure fair and reproducible comparisons, we evaluate all models using a subset of the publicly available UCL-SBM dataset that was used in Interspeech 2020 Computational Paralinguistics Challenge (ComParE2020), adhering to the challenge protocol. Our proposed WavLM-based model advances SOTA for this subset, achieving a PCC of 0.806.
evidence_items.title: Breathing Signal Prediction from Speech: Toward Reproducible and Comparable Models

evidence_items.summary: Dysarthria is a motor speech disorder that affects speech production, and severity assessment can benefit from combining acoustic and visual biomarkers. While recent advances have improved unimodal-based evaluations, most systems do not fully leverage facial motion, asymmetry, or the relationship between the produced speech and its intended linguistic content. In this work, we propose a framework for MultiModal Dysarthria Severity assessment (MMDyS), which exploits the alignment of speech, text, and visual biomarkers. We introduce a severity-conditioned contrastive objective that treats speech–text mismatch as a continuous signal of impairment, while the visual modality relies on hemiface lateralization to capture asymmetric articulatory patterns, complemented by temporal segmentation and flow motion descriptors. These representations are integrated through a mixture-of-experts mechanism with cross-modal alignment, enabling adaptive weighting of speech, text, and visual evidence. Evaluated on the Mandarin speech dysarthria multimodal (MSDM) benchmark, MMDyS achieves a subject-level macro F1 of 0.92 and the composite multimodal dysarthria severity assessment (MDSA) score of 11.7% over the current state-of-the-art. Our results show that modeling speech–text divergence and facial asymmetry leads to more informative and robust multimodal representations for dysarthria severity assessment. Code is available at: https://github.com/Lab-MSP/MMDyS.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Biomarkers of Dysarthria: Severity-Conditioned Contrastive Alignment of Speech, Text, and Facial Asymmetry

evidence_items.summary: Version 2 of the small-scaling benchmark dataset for joint Air Traffic Flow and Capacity Management (ATFCM): 200 small, tightly capacitated instances, small enough to be solved to optimality by exact methods, so that heuristics can be compared against proven optima. The instances were generated from real June 2019 traffic of the OpenSky Network with the open-source data generator ASPaeroFlow-DataGenerator v2.0.0. The dataset covers 5 regions (EAST-ASIA-3x3, CENTRAL-EUROPE-5x5, INDIA-4x10, USA-7x7, MAJOR-EUROPE-10x10), all on rectangular grids of synthetic navpoints, with 10 demand levels from 10 to 100 flights, 4 seeds and hourly timesteps. Capacities are set so that on average 31.8 % of the sectors are over capacity. Every instance holds the navigation graph, the sectors with their capacities and allocation, the airports, the aircraft and their filed flights for one 24-hour day, and an instance info.json with its parameters, generator commit and licence. The record also contains the unparsed output of the generator and its configurations. Compared with the first version, used in the LPNMR 2026 paper, the generator's demand model no longer discards the flights that cross UTC midnight, and destinations are drawn depending on origin and time of day. Licences: the instances are CC-BY-4.0, code is MIT. README.md describes the file formats, the formal model and how to cite it. The generator and the dataset are described in the paper "An Open-Source Data Generator for Joint Air Traffic Flow and Capacity Management Benchmarking" (preprint: 10.5281/zenodo.23039874); its large-scaling companion is 10.5281/zenodo.23039645 and benchmark results on both are 10.5281/zenodo.23039865.
evidence_items.title: Joint ATFCM benchmark instances V2 - small-scaling dataset

evidence_items.summary: Version 2 of the large-scaling benchmark dataset for joint Air Traffic Flow and Capacity Management (ATFCM): 6,720 solver-ready instances in which flights can be delayed or rerouted and airspace sectors reconfigured so that no sector exceeds its capacity. The instances were generated from real June 2019 traffic of the OpenSky Network with the open-source data generator ASPaeroFlow-DataGenerator v2.0.0. The dataset spans 8 regions on three continents, four rectangular grids (CENTRAL-EUROPE-7x7, USA-EAST-COAST-20x10, MAJOR-EUROPE-40x20, EAST-ASIA-40x40) and four Gabriel graphs on real waypoints (DACH, EUROPE, USA-MAINLAND, CENTRAL-EUROPE), at 4 time granularities (1, 4, 15 and 60 timesteps per hour), 7 demand levels (1,000 to 31,622 flights per day), 3 seeds and 10 capacity levels (10 % to 100 % of the nominal capacity). Every instance holds the navigation graph, the sectors with their capacities and allocation, the airports, the aircraft and their filed flights for one 24-hour day, and an instance info.json with its parameters, generator commit and licence. Every instance passes the generator's instance checker: trajectories follow graph edges inside the 24-hour window, and each aircraft's next leg departs from the airport where its previous leg landed. The record also contains the unparsed output of the generator, its configurations and every third-party input (OpenSky flight list, OurAirports snapshot, X-Plane navigation data), so the dataset can be regenerated from scratch. Compared with the first version, used in the ATMOS 2026 paper, the generator's demand model no longer discards the flights that cross UTC midnight, and destinations are drawn depending on origin and time of day. Licences: the four grid regions are CC-BY-4.0; the four regions built on real X-Plane waypoints are GPL-2.0-or-later; code is MIT (see LICENSING.md). README.md describes the file formats, the formal model, the fidelity of the data and how to cite it.
evidence_items.title: Joint ATFCM benchmark instances V2 - large-scaling dataset

evidence_items.summary: Publicly available Arabic datasets for target-specific stance detection remain limited, particularly for evaluating cross-target generalization. This paper presents the Mawqif-XT, consisting of 996 manually annotated Arabic tweets collected from three public targets: Women Driving, E-Cars, and Trimester System. Each tweet is annotated with stance, sentiment, and sarcasm labels following the original Mawqif annotation scheme. The released extension is intended as a held-out evaluation set for assessing model generalization to both semantically related and previously unseen targets, while the original Mawqif dataset is used for training and development. In addition, we establish baseline results using several Arabic and multilingual transformer models, as well as zero-shot large language models (LLMs), to facilitate reproducible evaluation. Together with the original Mawqif dataset, the Mawqif-v2 Extension provides a benchmark for evaluating cross-target generalization in Arabic stance detection.
evidence_items.title: Mawqif-XT: An Arabic Benchmark Dataset for Cross-Target Stance Detection

evidence_items.summary: Geo-Foundation Models (GFMs) have been evaluated across diverse Earth observation tasks and domains, showing strong potential to produce reliable maps even with sparse labels. However, systematic benchmarking of GFMs for Cryosphere applications remains limited, primarily because suitable evaluation datasets are scarce. We address this gap by introducing Cryo-Bench, a benchmark comprising six semantic segmentation datasets covering five cryospheric components: supraglacial debris, glacial lakes under two sensing configurations, sea ice, calving fronts and Antarctic ice-shelf extent. The benchmark includes multispectral, RGB, and synthetic aperture radar observations from regions underrepresented in existing pretraining archives. We evaluate thirteen GFMs alongside U-Net and Vision Transformer baselines trained from scratch under a unified evaluation protocol. With frozen encoders, the U-Net achieves the highest six-dataset average mean intersection over union (mIoU) of 69.31\%, exceeding TerraMind (67.86\%) by 1.45 points. The paired difference has a 95\% confidence interval of [+0.94, +1.98], indicating that the U-Net's lead is statistically significant. In contrast, learning-rate optimization substantially improves fine-tuning performance: DOFA reaches 93.97\% mIoU on the RGB glacial lake task, ranking the U-Net fourth, while Scale-MAE and GFM-Swin surpass U-Net on calving fronts. Averaged across all six datasets, four GFMs, TerraMind, GFM-Swin, DOFA, and Scale-MAE, exceed the U-Net baseline (69.31\%). In the few-shot setting, five GFMs, DOFA, RemoteCLIP, TerraMind, GFM-Swin, and Scale-MAE, likewise outperform U-Net; averaged across all thirteen GFMs, retention is 92.5\% of full-label accuracy compared with 86.1\% for U-Net.
evidence_items.title: Cryo-Bench: Benchmarking Foundation Models for Cryosphere Mapping

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning capabilities in complex tasks. However, they still struggle with hallucinations and factual errors in knowledge-intensive scenarios like knowledge graph question answering (KGQA). We attribute this to the semantic gap between structured knowledge graphs (KGs) and unstructured queries, caused by inherent differences in their focuses and structures. Existing methods usually employ resource-intensive, non-scalable workflows reasoning on vanilla KGs, but overlook this gap. To address this challenge, we propose a flexible framework, Enrich-on-Graph (EoG), which leverages LLMs' prior knowledge to enrich KGs, bridge the semantic gap between graphs and queries. EoG enables efficient evidence extraction from KGs for precise and robust reasoning, while ensuring low computational costs, scalability, and adaptability across different methods. Furthermore, we propose three graph quality evaluation metrics to analyze query-graph alignment in KGQA task, supported by theoretical validation of our optimization objectives. Extensive experiments on two KGQA benchmark datasets indicate that EoG can effectively generate high-quality KGs and achieve the state-of-the-art performance. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/zjukg/Enrich-on-Graph.
evidence_items.title: Enrich-on-Graph: Query-Graph Alignment for Complex Reasoning with LLM Enriching
